bib.title: Explanation in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Social Sciences
bib.venue: Artif. Intell. 2019 (the PDF is the arXiv v3 preprint, 'Preprint submitted to Journal Name', 15 Aug 2018)

question: What do philosophy, cognitive and social psychology say about how people define, generate, select, evaluate and present explanations, and how can explainable AI use it?
hypothesis: XAI should build on social-science models of human explanation rather than researchers' intuitions of a 'good' explanation.
contributions: Review of social-science work on explanation (over 250 publications surveyed, a subset presented)
Four major findings: explanations are contrastive, selected in a biased way, social, and probabilities matter less than causes
Per-section proposals for how each body of work applies to XAI

results.claim: Explanations are contrastive: people ask why P rather than Q.
results.source: Miller's synthesis of Hilton, Lipton, Hesslow and others
results.setup: Narrative review of mostly human-human explanation; not tested on ML users.
results.quote: people do not ask why event P happened, but rather why event P happened instead of some event Q

results.claim: Explanations are selected, in a biased manner; people give one or two causes.
results.setup: Same review; everyday (local) explanation.
results.quote: Humans are adept at selecting one or two causes from a sometimes inﬁnite number of causes to be the explanation.

results.claim: Probabilities matter but citing statistics is less effective than citing causes.
results.setup: Same review.
results.quote: referring to probabilities or statistical relationships in explanation is not as eﬀective as referring to causes

results.claim: Explanations are social: a transfer of knowledge in a conversation, not necessarily in natural language.
results.setup: Conversational model; footnote 2 and Sec 5.3.1 extend it to visual interaction.
results.quote: While Grice’s maxim are about conversation, they apply just as well to other modes of interaction.

results.claim: Over 250 social-science publications were surveyed; a subset is presented.
results.setup: Selection by 'currency and relevance'; no search protocol given.
results.quote: over 250 publications on explanation were surveyed from social science venues

results.claim: Showing a causal chain is attribution, not necessarily explanation.
results.setup: Aimed at lay users; most XAI work is attribution.
results.quote: Extracting a causal chain and displaying it to a person is causal attribution, not (neces- sarily) an explanation.

results.claim: People request only contrastive explanations (Miller's reading).
results.setup: Contested by Van Bouwel and Weber for plain-fact questions (p17).
results.quote: Research indicates that people request only contrastive explana- tions

results.claim: Contrastive answers can be easier: only the difference between fact and foil needs explaining.
results.setup: Holds, Miller says, for computational explanation too; no study given.
results.quote: one only needs to understand what is diﬀerent between the two cases

results.claim: Counterfactual (cause C absent) and foil (expected outcome Q) are different notions.
results.setup: Terminology adopted for the paper.
results.quote: we will adopt this terminology and use counterfactual to refer to the hypothetical case in which the cause C did not occur, and foil to refer to the hypothesised case Q that was expected rather than P.

results.claim: Likelihood does not strongly correlate with explanations people find useful; simplicity, generality, coherence matter at least as much.
results.setup: Review.
results.quote: While likely causes are part of good explanations, they do not strongly correlate with explanations that people ﬁnd useful.

results.claim: People favour simple explanations even when less likely; base rates reduce the effect.
results.setup: Patient symptom vignettes.
results.quote: Without base-rate information, participants selected the most simple (less likely) explanations. When base-rate information was included, this still occurred, but the diﬀerence was less pronounced.

results.claim: Completeness mattered more than soundness; sound but incomplete explanations were least preferred.
results.setup: Explanatory debugging of personalised song recommendations; participants' mental models measured.
results.quote: Sound but incomplete explanations were the least preferred, resulting in higher costs and more requests for clariﬁcation. Overall, Kulesza et al. concluded that completeness was more important than soundness.

results.claim: Principles of explanatory debugging: be sound, be complete, don't overwhelm.
results.setup: Principles 1 and 2 conflict with 3.
results.quote: (1) Be sound; (2) Be complete; but (3) Don’t over- whelm.

results.claim: A causal chain for a short story holds over 20 events and 30 causes.
results.setup: Kahneman and Tversky 'Mr. Jones' accident vignette.
results.quote: the causal chain consists of over 20 events and 30 causes, all relevant to the accident

results.claim: Responsibility of C for E is 1/(N+1), N the minimal changes needed to prevent E.
results.setup: Gerstenberg and Lagnado 2010: predicted ratings better than simple counterfactual and matching models in a team triangle-counting game.
results.quote: If N is the minimal number of changes required, then the responsibility of C causes E is 1 N+1. If N = 0, then C is fully responsible.
results.note: Extraction flattens the fraction; printed as 1/(N+1).

results.claim: Knobe effect: 82% said harm was intentional, 23% said help was.
results.setup: Chairman vignette; harm vs help as side effect.
results.quote: 82% of respondents replied yes. However, in the second vignette, only 23% thought that the chairman intentionally helped the environment.

results.claim: Non-permitted actor rated more than three times stronger as cause when the outcome was negative.
results.setup: Stationery-cupboard scenario; only slightly stronger for a positive outcome.
results.quote: participants rated the action of the non-permitted actor (e.g. Professor Smith) more than three times stronger than the other actor

results.claim: Explaining during category learning aided generalisation but hurt exceptions.
results.setup: Explain vs think-aloud groups.
results.quote: the explanation group more accurately categorised features that had similar patterns to the training examples, but less accurately categorised exceptional cases

results.claim: Irrelevant information dilutes relevant information; effect vanished when conversational maxims were deactivated.
results.source: Tetlock and Boettger 1989; Tetlock et al.
results.setup: Predicting David's GPA; study hours 3 or 31 per week.
results.quote: the dilution eﬀect disappeared when conversational maxims were deactivated

results.claim: Existing ML work selects important features but none uses human cognitive biases to select explanations (as of 2018).
results.setup: Statement about the field in 2018.
results.quote: as far as the authors are aware, there are currently no studies that look at the cognitive biases of humans as a way to select explanations from a set of causes

results.claim: Default foil proposal: read 'Why P?' as 'Why P rather than the normal case Q?'.
results.setup: Illustrated with glaucoma risk; not evaluated.
results.quote: Why P rather than the normal case Q?

results.claim: Unprompted explanation with every decision risks becoming less needed and more distracting.
results.setup: Argument, not tested.
results.quote: runs a risk of providing explanations that become less needed and more distracting over time

limits: A review plus argument: its XAI points are mostly 'I argue' proposals; it is expressly not a survey of existing XAI approaches (p6).
No pooled effect sizes, study sample sizes or search protocol; selection of the subset by 'currency and relevance' (p4).
Scope is everyday (local) explanation of particular events for lay explainees, not scientific or global explanation (p5).
Contrastiveness is contested: Van Bouwel and Weber reject that all plain-fact questions have an implicit foil (p17).
Author concedes: 'I acknowledge that incorporating these ideas are not feasible for all applications' (p59).
Trust vs truth: a persuasive, less likely explanation may be better for trust (p15, p49); this is acceptance, not calibrated trust.
Dated: 2018 text; predates SHAP-era and LLM explanation user studies. SHAP does not appear; LIME only as ref [157].
practices: Treat causal attribution as only part of explanation; add selection and presentation (Sec 2.6.1).
Support contrastive questions and, where the foil is implicit, elicit or infer it, e.g. from abnormality or default 'normal case' foils (Sec 2.6.2, 4.6.3).
State which level of explanation (material, formal, efficient, final) a method addresses (Sec 2.6.3).
Keep a model of self for explanation, which may only approximate the decision model (Sec 2.6.4).
Select explanation causes using abnormality, intentionality, controllability, recency and fact-foil differences (Sec 4.6.2-4.6.5).
Weigh simplicity, generality and coherence alongside likelihood when the goal is understanding or trust (Sec 4.6.6).
Make explanation interactive and obey Gricean maxims, whatever the medium (Sec 5.3.1).
Avoid diluting key causes with less relevant parts of a chain (Sec 5.3.5).

terms.definition: an answer to a why-question; also a cognitive process and a social process
the fact is the event that did occur (P); the foil is the hypothesised case Q that was expected rather than P
the hypothetical case in which the cause C did not occur
identifying the causes of an event; one part of the whole process of explanation

Biran and Cotton's definition adopted: the degree to which an observer can understand the cause of a decision; Miller equates it with explainability and treats explanation as post-hoc interpretability
explains why a decision is good, not necessarily the actual decision-making process
what (associative), how (interventionist), why (counterfactual), after Pearl and Mackenzie's ladder

terms.term: causal connection / explanation selection / explanation evaluation
terms.definition: identifying causes; choosing a subset as the explanation; judging its quality
irrelevant information weakens the effect of relevant information
